title: Robert the Bruce and the Spider
text:
In 1306 Robert the Bruce had himself crowned King of Scots in defiance of Edward I of England. Within months he was beaten at Methven and again at Dalrigh. His supporters were killed or captured, his wife and daughter were taken prisoner, and three of his brothers were later executed. Bruce went into hiding, probably on the western isles or in Ireland, through the winter.

A well-known story, which Walter Scott retold for children in his Tales of a Grandfather in 1828, comes from this period. Lying in a poor hut and wondering whether to give up the struggle, Bruce watched a spider trying to swing from one roof beam to another to fix its web. It tried six times and failed six times. Bruce reflected that he too had fought six times against the English and failed. He decided that if the spider tried a seventh time and succeeded, he would try again. The spider succeeded.

Whatever its origin, Bruce did return in 1307. He fought a long guerrilla war, took back castle after castle, and in 1314 defeated the English army at Bannockburn.
lesson: Repeated failure is not a verdict. Small reminders of persistence can carry you through the moment when quitting seems reasonable.
location: Scotland (traditionally a cave or hut in the west)
source: Walter Scott, Tales of a Grandfather (1828), from earlier Scottish tradition
caveat: The spider story first appears centuries later, and a similar tale was told of Bruce's companion James Douglas.
